# Cycle 0001 Insight

## Cohort outcome

The cohort tried three changes to how items move between the probing, stash, and normal tiers: where a stash-promoted item lands in its target bucket, whether a probing hit re-inserts the item, and whether foreign evictions skip the retry in their true target. Only v002, the change to the landing slot for stash hits, won; the other two regressed on hit-rate and were not winners.

## Patterns

- Landing position matters more than movement. Moving a re-referenced stash item to the MRU end of its target bucket was the only change that helped, while the two changes that added movement or removed a retry both hurt hit-rate.
- Keeping residency in the probing tier appears valuable. Removing and re-inserting probing hits pushed proven-hot keys back through target competition and lost ground.
- Shortening the demotion path alone does not pay off. Skipping the target retry for foreign evictions lowered the one measured dimension, and the predicted per-op-time gain was never recorded.
- The winner's evidence is thin. Its only measured dimension is hit-rate, on a single workload, so the win is a hit-rate result, not a demonstrated overall improvement.
- Rationale is inconsistently documented around the winning change. The Front/Back default is described differently in different places, which makes the intent of v002 harder for later cycles to verify.

## Open questions

- Does the MRU landing for stash hits hold on workloads other than the LIRS trace used here?
- Do per-op-time and metadata-size move at all under any of these changes? No variant measured them.
- Would the removed target retry pay for itself if the shorter eviction path is paired with better stash capacity handling?

## Continuation

Next cycle should build on v002: vary the stash-hit landing slot further and measure it across more workloads, plus per-op-time and metadata-size. Drop the probing-hit remove-and-reinsert idea and the direct-to-stash eviction change unless a follow-up explicitly measures the costs they were meant to offset.

# Cycle 0002 Insight

## Cohort outcome

The cohort tried three changes around stash promotion and foreign-eviction placement: gating stash promotion on a second hit, making the stash-hit landing slot depend on target-bucket occupancy, and restoring the target retry for foreign evictions only when the stash is full. Only v001 is listed as a Winner, and its measured hit-rate matched its parent, so the win is inherited rather than new.

## Patterns

- The one clear hit-rate gain came from admission filtering. Requiring a second hit before a stash item is promoted helped on the LIRS trace, which suggests one-off stash hits were displacing resident items.
- Refinements of the landing slot changed nothing measurable. The occupancy-conditional landing matched its parent, so the cohort gives no evidence that the full-bucket case it targets is common on this workload.
- Gating the direct-to-stash shortcut on free stash capacity recovered only a small part of the hit-rate lost by the unconditional shortcut. That supports the view that stash pressure is what made the removed retry valuable.
- Every variant was judged on hit-rate alone. Per-op-time and metadata-size were measured in none of them, so no cost of the promotion filter or its marker is known.
- Several insights rest on the hypothesis text rather than the overlay diff, so the implementations are not confirmed as described.

## Open questions

- Is v001 a Winner against the baseline, or only against its parent v002? Its own insight reports no change from that parent.
- Does the second-hit promotion filter hold on workloads other than the LIRS trace?
- Does the one-bit seen-in-stash marker stay within existing entry metadata, and what does it cost in per-op-time?
- Is the occupancy-conditional landing ever triggered on any workload?

## Continuation

Next cycle should build on the second-hit promotion filter: test it on more than one workload and measure per-op-time and metadata-size alongside hit-rate. Drop the occupancy-conditional landing refinement, since it showed no effect, and treat the capacity-gated direct-to-stash path as a secondary lever to revisit only if the promotion filter's cost is measured.

# Cycle 0003 Insight

## Cohort outcome

The cohort tried three changes around the one-bit "seen in stash" marker: stacking the second-hit promotion gate on the MRU stash-hit landing, using the marker to prefer never-re-hit stash entries as eviction victims, and moving the marker into a spare tag or bitmap bit. Only v001 won, and its gain is a small hit-rate improvement on a single trace.

## Patterns

- Stacking the two stash-hit levers looks complementary. The second-hit gate added on top of MRU landing gave a small gain, but it has been measured on only one workload and one capacity.
- Using the marker as an eviction signal hurt. Preferring never-re-hit stash entries as victims discarded recently arrived items that had not yet had a chance to prove reuse.
- The marker-relocation variant reports no hit-rate change. Its evidence does not show whether the marker moved into a spare bit at all, or whether the variant fell back to no change, so its cost is unknown.
- Metadata-size and per-op-time were not measured in any variant, so the cost side of the marker work remains unverified.

## Open questions

- Does the stacked second-hit gate with MRU landing hold on workloads and capacities other than the LIRS trace at size 2048?
- Did the spare-bit variant actually change the entry layout, and if so, what happens to metadata-size?
- Is the victim-preference idea dead, or does it only fail when the marker is the sole criterion?

## Continuation

Next cycle should build on v001: keep the MRU landing with the second-hit gate, and test it across more workloads and capacities while measuring metadata-size and per-op-time. Drop the never-re-hit eviction-victim preference. Verify the spare-bit variant's diff before spending further cycles on marker relocation.

# Cycle 0004 Insight

## Cohort outcome

The cohort tried three changes around the seen-in-stash marker and stash handling: making the second-hit promotion gate depend on stash occupancy, relocating the marker into a spare tag bit, and changing stash-tier victim selection to the earliest-landed entry in the target bucket. Only v001 is listed as a Winner, but its measured hit-rate is effectively unchanged from its parent, so no variant produced a new measurable gain.

## Patterns

- The occupancy-conditional promotion gate matched its parent on the one measured trace. Pressure-specific gating added no visible value on this workload and capacity.
- Relocating the marker into a spare tag bit left hit-rate exactly unchanged. This is consistent with a pure layout change, but it does not show that any metadata saving was realized.
- Changing stash victim order to earliest-landed produced exactly baseline hit-rate. Eviction-order tweaks in this part of the design have shown no effect so far.
- Across all three variants, no change moved hit-rate, and metadata-size and per-op-time were measured in none. The cost side of every change is unknown.
- Two insights rest on hypothesis text rather than the overlay diff, so the implementations are not confirmed as described.

## Open questions

- Why is v001 a Winner when its insight reports no change from its parent? Is it winning against a baseline, or only carried forward?
- Does any of this cohort's behaviour hold on workloads or capacities other than the LIRS trace at size 2048?
- Did the spare-bit variant actually pack the marker, and if so, what happens to metadata-size?
- Does earliest-landed victim selection ever differ from the current selection on any workload?

## Continuation

Next cycle should not spend more effort on small landing, promotion-gate, or victim-order refinements, since this cohort found none that move hit-rate on the single trace. Instead, it should test the v001 lineage on more workloads and capacities and record metadata-size and per-op-time, so the cost side of the marker work is finally measured. Drop the occupancy-conditional gate and the earliest-landed victim change unless a follow-up shows a measurable effect.

# Cycle 0005 Insight

## Cohort outcome

The cohort tried three changes: a ghost-history fast path for readmitting recently evicted keys, an equivalence-preserving occupancy counter for victim search, and moving probing-tier demotions to the LRU end of their normal-tier bucket. Only v001 is listed as a Winner, yet its own insight reports a slight hit-rate drop on the one measured trace, so the Winner status is not supported by this cohort's evidence.

## Patterns

- Early readmission looks harmful. The ghost-history path let returning keys skip the seen-in-stash wait, and the result was a slight hit-rate loss, which suggests recently evicted keys displaced residents that were still earning their place.
- The two no-change variants agree with each other. The occupancy-counter refactor and the demotion-placement change both matched the parent exactly, so this cohort gives no evidence that victim-search cost or demoted-item placement moves hit-rate on this workload.
- No variant measured per-op-time or metadata-size. The occupancy counter's claimed speedup and the ghost set's memory cost are both untested.
- Three of three insights rest partly on hypothesis text because the overlay diffs were not readable. The implementations are not confirmed as described.

## Open questions

- Why is v001 listed as a Winner when its measured hit-rate is below its parent? Is it winning against a different baseline?
- Does the occupancy counter produce any speedup once per-op-time is measured?
- Is demoted-item placement ever the deciding factor for a victim on any workload or capacity?
- Does the ghost-history cost in metadata justify any hit-rate it might gain on other traces?

## Continuation

Next cycle should not pursue the ghost-history fast path further unless a second workload shows a clear hit-rate gain, since the one measured result was negative. Drop the demotion-placement change, which showed no effect. Keep the occupancy counter only as a cost-side experiment: re-test it with per-op-time and metadata-size recorded, and confirm the overlay diffs before drawing conclusions.

# Cycle 0006 Insight

## Cohort outcome

The cohort tried three changes around the stash promotion gate and the victim-side bookkeeping: replacing the one-bit seen-in-stash marker with a 2-bit saturating reuse counter (v001), reordering the promotion gate so the marker is read only at high occupancy (v002), and replacing a slot scan in eviction with a per-bucket occupancy counter (v003). Only v001 is a Winner, and its hit-rate gain over the parent is marginal on a single trace.

## Patterns

- The saturating reuse counter is the only change with any hit-rate signal, and it is weak. Gating promotion on persistent reuse rather than a single re-hit may matter, but one workload and one run cannot separate it from noise.
- The reorder and the occupancy counter both matched their parent exactly. That is consistent with behaviour-preserving refactors, but neither variant recorded per-op-time or metadata-size, so their claimed speed and layout benefits are unmeasured.
- Across the cohort, no variant recorded metadata-size or per-op-time. The cost side of the reuse counter, which adds bits per entry, is therefore unknown.
- None of the three insights confirms the overlay diff. Each describes the intended change, so the implementations are not verified as written.

## Open questions

- Does the reuse-counter gain hold on workloads or capacities other than the LIRS trace at size 2048?
- Does the 2-bit counter's metadata cost justify any hit-rate gain it shows?
- Do the occupancy counter and the reordered gate reduce per-op-time once that metric is recorded?
- Is the counter reset on demotion and eviction implemented as specified?

## Continuation

Next cycle should pursue the saturating reuse counter from v001 as the single lead, and test it on more workloads and capacities while recording hit-rate, metadata-size, and per-op-time. Drop the gate reorder, which showed no effect. Keep the occupancy counter only as a cost-side check that records per-op-time, and verify the overlay diffs before drawing conclusions from any variant.

# Cycle 0007 Insight

## Cohort outcome

The cohort tried three reuse-tracking and admission tweaks: restricting reuse-counter increments to hits on entries last touched before the immediately preceding access (v001), halving rather than zeroing the reuse counter on normal-tier demotion (v002), and dropping probing-tier exits that have zero probing hits instead of moving them to the stash (v003). Only v002 is listed as a Winner, yet its own insight reports a change within noise on the one measured trace, so the Winner status is not supported by this cohort's evidence.

## Patterns

- All three changes are flat on the single measured trace. None of the reuse-counter or admission refinements moved hit-rate beyond noise on LIRS workload-a at size 2048.
- The reuse-counter lineage has now shown no signal in two cycles. The partial-credit-on-demotion idea (v002) and the back-to-back filter (v001) both returned parent-level results, which weakens the case for the saturating-counter direction from Cycle 0006 on this workload.
- The probing-tier admission filter (v003) also left hit-rate flat, so stash-pressure relief is not visible as a hit-rate lever here.
- No insight reports metadata-size or per-op-time, so the cost side of every variant remains unmeasured.
- In all three cases the overlay sources could not be read, so the insights describe intended changes rather than verified implementations.

## Open questions

- Why is v002 a Winner when its measured change is within noise? Is it winning against a different baseline, or carried forward?
- Does the reuse-counter direction produce any gain on a second workload or capacity, given three cycles of flat or marginal results on the one trace?
- Does the probing-tier filter's bypassed-entry count show any stash-pressure effect that hit-rate alone does not capture?
- Are the reset-on-demotion and back-to-back gating sites implemented as hypothesized?

## Continuation

Next cycle should stop refining reuse-counter increments, reset timing, and probing-tier admission on the single LIRS trace, since none has moved hit-rate. If the reuse-counter lineage is kept at all, test its best existing form on a second workload and capacity while recording metadata-size and per-op-time, and drop the back-to-back filter and the probing-tier admission filter.

# Cycle 0008 Insight

## Cohort outcome

The cohort tried three changes: gating probing-origin stash promotions on a saturated reuse counter (v001), skipping the reuse-counter store on hits to already-saturated entries (v002), and shifting 128 slots from the probing tier to the stash (v003). Only v002 is listed as a Winner, yet its own insight reports hit-rate unchanged from the parent and no per-op-time measurement, so the Winner status is not supported by this cohort's evidence.

## Patterns

- The reuse-counter direction is flat again. The saturated-counter promotion gate (v001) left hit-rate within noise on LIRS workload-a at size 2048, which is the fourth cycle in a row where refinements of reuse tracking show no hit-rate signal on that trace.
- The store-skip change (v002) matched its parent exactly. That fits a behaviour-preserving change, but its claimed cost benefit is unmeasured because per-op-time is not in the fitness vector.
- Shrinking the probing tier to grow the stash (v003) lost hit-rate. The probing tier does not look oversized, and stash pressure does not look like the binding constraint on this trace.
- No variant recorded metadata-size or per-op-time, so the cost side of the whole cohort is still unknown.
- None of the three insights confirms the overlay source. Each describes the intended change, so the implementations are not verified as written.

## Open questions

- Why is v002 a Winner when its measured hit-rate is identical to the parent? Is it carried forward for its cost claim, which has not been measured?
- Does any reuse-counter variant gain hit-rate on a second workload or capacity, given four cycles of flat or marginal results on one trace?
- Would a probing-tier capacity change in the opposite direction help, or is the split already at a reasonable point?
- Is the store-skip and saturated-gate logic implemented as hypothesized?

## Continuation

Next cycle should stop refining reuse-counter gates and store behaviour on the single LIRS trace, and should drop the probing-to-stash capacity shift. If any cost-side experiment continues, record per-op-time and metadata-size and verify the overlay diffs first. If the reuse-counter lineage is kept at all, test its best existing form on a second workload and capacity before proposing further variants.

# Cycle 0009 Insight

## Cohort outcome

The cohort tried three changes: collapsing the saturating reuse counter into the one-bit seen-in-stash marker (v001), adding an equivalence-preserving occupancy check that skips slot scans which cannot find a free slot (v002), and moving 128 slots from the stash back to the probing tier at fixed total capacity (v003). Only v003 is a Winner, on a small hit-rate gain over its parent on the single LIRS trace at size 2048.

## Patterns

- The capacity move is the only change with a hit-rate signal. Reversing the cycle 0008 shrink of the probing tier improved hit-rate, which is the opposite of what that shrink produced. Together the two results point to probing residency, not stash capacity, as the binding resource on this trace.
- The reuse-counter direction is again weak. Removing the counter's extra states (v001) produced a small drop just outside tolerance, so the counter may carry minor signal, but the effect is small and on one trace.
- The occupancy check (v002) matched its parent exactly, as a victim-preserving change should. Its cost benefit is unmeasured because per-op-time is absent from the fitness vector.
- No variant recorded metadata-size or per-op-time, so the cost side of the cohort is still unknown, including the bit cost of the reuse counter.
- None of the three insights confirms the overlay source. The v003 reading is tied to the stated change, not to verified constants, so the winning implementation is not yet checked.

## Open questions

- Is the v003 gain larger than trace-level noise, and does it hold on a second workload or capacity?
- Where is the probing-tier optimum? The gain from growing probing may flatten or reverse beyond 128 slots.
- Does the small v001 drop indicate a real loss of reuse-depth information, and is it worth the metadata it costs?
- Do the occupancy skip and the probing resize stay consistent with the stash-full retry and derived sizes?

## Continuation

Next cycle should pursue the probing-tier capacity increase from v003 as the lead, and test a few sizes around it on a second workload while recording hit-rate, metadata-size, and per-op-time. Drop the seen-in-stash collapse from v001, since it did not help and the reuse-counter lineage has shown no robust signal. Keep the occupancy check only as a cost-side check that records per-op-time, and verify the overlay diffs before treating v003 as settled.

# Cycle 0010 Insight

## Cohort outcome

The cohort tried three changes: moving a further 128 slots from the stash to the probing tier, for a 256-slot total shift (v001), folding the seen-in-stash marker into spare bits of the slot record (v002), and gating stash promotion on a second hit that falls within a recency window (v003). None of the three improved hit-rate against its parent on the single LIRS trace at size 2048. Only v003 is listed as a Winner, yet its own insight reports a hit-rate loss, so the Winner status is not supported by this cohort's evidence.

## Patterns

- The probing-tier gain from cycle 0009 does not extend. Pushing the shift to 256 slots (v001) lost hit-rate, so the benefit of probing residency saturates at or before that point and the stash capacity given up becomes the larger cost.
- Recency is not the promotion signal. Requiring a close-in-time second hit before promotion (v003) lost hit-rate, which suggests the current promotion behaviour is doing useful work that a recency gate removes.
- The marker fold (v002) matched its parent exactly. That fits a layout-only change, but its metadata-size benefit was never measured.
- No variant recorded metadata-size or per-op-time, so the cost side of the cohort is still unknown.
- None of the three insights confirms the overlay source. Each reads the result against the stated change, so the implementations are not verified as written.

## Open questions

- Where is the probing-tier optimum? Is it at 128 slots, or is there a peak between 128 and 256 that a finer sweep would find?
- Why is v003 a Winner when its measured hit-rate fell? Is it carried forward against a different baseline, or is the designation an error?
- Does the recency gate fail on other workloads or sizes, or is it a trace-specific loss?
- Does the marker fold's metadata saving justify the change if it is never measured?

## Continuation

Next cycle should stop growing the probing tier beyond the 128-slot shift and drop the second-hit recency gate from v003. Keep the 128-slot probing split as the lead, sweep a few sizes near it on a second workload, and record hit-rate, metadata-size, and per-op-time. Re-check v003's Winner designation before building on it.
